''Zappania citrodora'' Lam. |synonyms_ref = {{GRIN | access-date=2010-04-12}} }} '''''Aloysia citrodora''''', '''lemon verbena''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[verbena]] [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] Verbenaceae, [[native plant|native]] to South America. Other common names include '''lemon beebrush'''.{{cite journal |author1=Armada, J. |author2=A. Barra |title=On ''Aloysia'' Palau (Verbenaceae) |year=1992 |journal=[[Taxon (journal)|Taxon]] |volume=41 |issue=1 |pages=88–90 |jstor=1222497|doi=10.2307/1222497}} It was brought to [[Europe]] by the [[Spain|Spanish]] and the [[Portugal|Portuguese]] in the 17th century and cultivated for its oil.{{cite book|author=Margaret Joan Roberts|author-link=Margaret Roberts (herbalist)|title=Margaret Roberts' A–Z Herbs: Identifying Herbs, How to Grow Herbs, the Uses of Herbs|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YdWEcMjKVBYC&pg=PA51|year=2000|publisher=Struik|isbn=978-1-86872-499-4|page=51}} ==Description== Lemon verbena is a [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[shrub]] or [[subshrub]] growing to {{convert|2–3|m|ft|0}} high. The {{convert|8|cm|in|-long|adj=mid|frac=2}}, glossy, pointed leaves are slightly rough to the touch and emit a strong [[lemon]] scent when bruised (hence the Latin [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''citrodora''—lemon-scented).{{cite book|last=Harrison|first=Lorraine|title=RHS Latin for gardeners|year=2012|publisher=Mitchell Beazley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=9781845337315|pages=224}} Sprays of tiny purple or white flowers appear in late spring or early summer, although potted lemon verbenas may not flower. It is evergreen in tropical locations,{{cite web |title=Aloysia citriodora - Plant Finder |url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=c962 |website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org |access-date=16 June 2019}} but is sensitive to cold, losing leaves at temperatures below 0 °C (32 °F), although the wood is hardy to −10 °C (14 °F).{{citation needed|date=June 2019}} Pruning is recommended in spring to encourage a bushy form.{{cite web |title=Lemon Verbena |url=https://www.abc.net.au/gardening/factsheets/lemon-verbena/9424018 |publisher=Australian Broadcasting Corporation |access-date=16 June 2019 |language=en-AU |date=21 May 2005}} Due to its many culinary uses, it is widely listed and marketed as a plant for the herb garden. Researchers have identified [[anxiolytic]] effects in rat models.{{cite journal |last1=Abouyaala |first1=Oumaima |last2=Bougrine |first2=Soukaina |last3=Brikat |first3=Sara |last4=Brouzi |first4=Mohammed yassine El |last5=Elhessni |first5=Aboubaker |last6=Mesfioui |first6=Abdelhalem |last7=Ouahidi |first7=Moulay Laarbi |title=The anxiolytic, anti-depressive, and antioxidative effects of lemon verbena in rat rendered diabetic by streptozotocin injection |journal=Neuroscience and Behavioral Physiology |date=6 January 2025 |doi=10.1007/s11055-024-01711-w}} ==Uses== [[File:IncaKolaBottleGlass.jpg|200px|right|thumb|[[Inca Kola]] soft drink, which is flavored with lemon verbena.]] Lemon verbena leaves are used to add a lemon flavor to [[Fish as food|fish]] and [[poultry]] dishes, vegetable [[marinade]]s, [[salad dressing]]s, jams, puddings, [[Greek yogurt]], and beverages.{{cite book |last1=Small |first1=Ernest |title=Culinary herbs |date=2006 |publisher=[[National Research Council of Canada]] |location=Ottawa, Ontario |isbn=0-660-19073-7 |pages=145–150 |edition=Second}} The leaves are also used in [[potpourri]]. Lemon verbena is used to make [[herbal tea]]s and as a [[liqueur]] flavoring. It is used in [[traditional medicine]] in [[Latin America|Latin American countries]].{{cite journal |last1=Bahramsoltani |first1=Roodabeh |last2=Rostamiasrabadi |first2=Pourouchista |last3=Shahpiri |first3=Zahra |last4=Marques |first4=André M. |last5=Rahimi |first5=Roja |last6=Farzaei |first6=Mohammad Hosein |title=Aloysia citrodora Paláu (Lemon verbena): A review of phytochemistry and pharmacology |journal=[[Journal of Ethnopharmacology]] |date=August 2018 |volume=222 |pages=34–51 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2018.04.021 |pmid=29698776}} The oil was historically steam-distilled from the leaves for use in the perfume industry, but it has skin-sensitising and [[Phototoxicity|phototoxic]] properties.{{cite book |editor1-last=Groom |editor1-first=Nigel |editor-link=Nigel Groom |title=The new perfume handbook |publisher=Blackie Academic & Professional |isbn=9780751404036 |page=344 |edition=2nd}} In the [[European Union]], verbena [[essential oil]]s (''Lippia citriodora'' Kunth.) and derivatives other than absolute are prohibited when used as a fragrance ingredient (Regulation No. 1223/2009, Annex II).{{cite web |title=Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on cosmetic products |url=https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:02009R1223-20191218 |publisher=EUR-Lex |access-date=2 June 2020}} ==Chemistry== The major isolates in lemon verbena oil are [[citral]] (30–35%), [[nerol]], and [[geraniol]].Lawless, J., ''The Illustrated Encyclopedia of Essential Oils'', {{ISBN|1-85230-661-0}} {{page needed|date=June 2019}} Extracts of lemon verbena also contain [[verbascoside]], an antimicrobial. As the plant has several [[phytochemical]]s which may act as [[Substrate (chemistry)|substrate]]s for [[Drug metabolism|drug-metabolizing]] enzymes, lemon verbena may cause [[herb-drug interactions]]. However, lemon verbena oil is generally recognized as safe ([[GRAS]]) by the US [[Food and Drug Administration]] when used as a flavoring.{{cite web |title=Substances Added to Food (formerly EAFUS) 25, 2020|publisher=US Food and Drug Administration|date=22 April 2019}} ==Synonyms== Synonyms for lemon verbena are ''[[Verbena]] triphylla'' L'Hér.,{{cite web |title=ITIS Standard Report Page: Aloysia citrodora |url=https://www.itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?search_topic=TSN&search_value=832759#null |website=[[www.itis.gov]] |access-date=16 June 2019}} ''Verbena citriodora'' Cav.,{{citation needed|date=June 2019}} ''[[Lippia]] triphylla'', and ''Lippia citriodora''. ==Garden history== The first European botanist who publicly noticed this plant was the French [[Philibert Commerson]], who collected it in Buenos Aires on his botanical circumnavigation with [[Louis Antoine de Bougainville|Bougainville]], about 1767.{{failed verification|date=June 2019}} The plant had already been imported directly into the [[Real Jardín Botánico de Madrid]], where in 1797 professors [[Casimiro Gómez Ortega]] and {{ill|Antonio Palau y Verdera|es}} named it, though they did not yet effectively publish it, ''Aloysia citriodora'' in Latin and "Hierba de la Princesa" in Spanish,Juan Armada and Alfredo Barra, "On ''Aloysia'' Palau (''Verbenaceae'')", ''Taxon'' '''41''' (1992:88f), note a recently discovered anonymous six-page printed booklet, dated Madrid 1779, reporting the new species, which they assert is correctly ''Aloysia citrodora'' (Palau). to compliment [[Maria Louisa of Parma]], [[Princess of Asturias]] the wife of the Garden's patron [[Charles IV of Spain|Infante Carlos de Borbon]], [[Prince of Asturias]] and son of king Carlos III."''un nuevo génera de planta consagrado a la Princesa de Asturias nuestra señora''" in the title of the anonymous booklet. The name was later effectively published in the first volume of Palau's ''Parte Práctica de Botánica'' in 1784.{{citation needed|date=June 2019}} Unofficial importations from Spanish America seldom fared well: when another French botanist [[Joseph Dombey]] landed his collections at [[Cádiz]] in 1785, the plants were impounded and left to rot in warehouses, while Dombey was refused permission even to have seeds planted. Among the bare handful of plants Dombey had assembled during eight years at Lima, lemon verbena survived.{{citation needed|date=June 2019}} Gómez Ortega sent seeds and specimens of the plant to [[Charles Louis L'Héritier de Brutelle]] in Paris; L'Héritier published it as ''Verbena triphylla'' in his ''[[Stirpes Novae]]'', published in December 1785 or January 1786. From Paris [[John Sibthorp]], professor of botany at Oxford, obtained the specimen that he introduced to British horticulture:{{cite web |title=Plant of the Month 2017 |url=https://www.soci.org/interest-groups/technical-groups/horticulture-group/plant-of-the-month-2017 |website=www.soci.org |publisher=[[Society of Chemical Industry]]}} by 1797 lemon verbena was common in greenhouses around London, and its popularity as essential in a fragrant bouquet increased through the following century.{{citation needed|date=June 2019}} This plant has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Aloysia citrodora''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/284648/Aloysia-citrodora/Details|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|access-date=9 April 2020}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons category}} * {{Wikispecies-inline|Aloysia citrodora}} {{Clear}} {{Herbs & spices}} {{Taxonbar |from = Q206532 }} [[Category:Aloysia|citrodora]] [[Category:Plants described in 1874]] [[Category:Flora of Argentina]] [[Category:Flora of Paraguay]] [[Category:Flora of Brazil]] [[Category:Flora of Chile]] [[Category:Flora of Peru]] [[Category:Herbs]] [[Category:Medicinal plants of South America]]
